Subject: Residency & Logging requirements — follow-up (Horizon Health)

Hi Maria,

Thanks again for taking the call earlier — appreciate the clear priorities. Quick written recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned: 

- Primary ask: US-only residency for patient PII (both at-rest and in-transit), with the ability to have a warm-standby in EU that does NOT contain replicated PII.
- Retention: you mentioned a 7-year retention requirement for records that contain patient identifiers; logs/audit trails should be retained for 3 years but we should confirm scope (access logs vs. full request bodies).
- Logging: need admin/audit logs accessible to your Security team, with tamper-evident storage and export support.
- Failover: prefer an automated failover policy that preserves residency guarantees (i.e., in an incident we want traffic to route within the US where possible; EU warm-standby only for non-PII metadata).
- Next steps I propose: SE technical write-up on how pinning & replication work + an operations diagram (Ben), a short procurement checklist for the SOW/contract (Monica), and a follow-up call to walk the security team through controls.

Questions we still need clarified from Horizon:
1) Can you list the specific fields you consider PII for this integration (e.g., MRN, SSN, birthdate)?
2) Is any subset of your traffic allowed to be processed outside the US (e.g., anonymized telemetry or embeddings)?
3) Do you require any specific certificate/KMS integrations (HSM / customer-managed keys)?
4) Who should be the procurement contact for the SOW and any addendum to the data residency clause?

I attached the call transcript and will follow up with Ben's one-pager on residency options tomorrow.

Best,
Logan Wright

Thanks, Logan — useful recap. I'm attaching a short spreadsheet with our answers and the fields we classify as PII (Horizon_Security_QA.xlsx). Quick answers inline below: 

- PII fields: patient full name, MRN, DOB, SSN, contact email/phone, insurance policy numbers. Any clinical notes that can be tied to a patient are also considered sensitive.
- Transmission/processing: All requests that include any of the above fields must remain within the US. We can consider anonymized telemetry (no patient identifiers) being processed outside the US for analytics.
- Warm-standby: We can accept an EU warm-standby as long as it never contains PII. The warm-standby can receive topology/state metadata but not full request payloads with identifiers.
- KMS: We prefer customer-managed keys for encryption-at-rest; our security team will want to review compat.
- Procurement: procurement@horizonhealth.com is the right inbox; I copied Raj for security follow-ups.

A couple of clarifying questions for Redwood: 
1) How do you segregate network egress to prevent cross-region replication of request bodies?
2) Are request-level logs (full request and response) stored by default, or just metadata (timestamps, IP, model used)?
3) If there's an automated failover, can we enforce a policy that prevents failover to any region outside the approved list unless there is a documented and auditable emergency?

We'll aim to have legal/security review the attached sheet today. If you can confirm answers to the three questions above, we'll pick a time for the next call.

Thanks — Maria

Subject: Re: Residency & Logging requirements — follow-up (Horizon Health)

Hi Maria — Ben (SE) here, following up with technical details and recommended options. Summary answers to your three questions, plus proposed config that meets Horizon's constraints.

1) Preventing cross-region replication of request bodies:
- Redwood supports per-customer pinning that binds request payload storage to a geographic region. For Horizon we can pin workloads to US-only datastores; warm-standby nodes in EU will only have encrypted metadata and route tables, not decrypted request payloads.
- Network egress controls: we offer VPC peering and private endpoints with egress policies that deny outbound replication to non-approved regions unless an explicit org-level override is enabled.

2) Default logging behavior:
- Default: request metadata (timestamp, route, model, token count) retained for diagnostic reasons; full request/response bodies are retained only if customer enables full-content logging. For Horizon's default profile we will disable full-content request logging.
- Audit/admin logs (who accessed key ops, config changes) are retained and can be exported. We can set retention to 3 years for audit logs per your ask.

3) Failover enforcement:
- Failover policies are policy-driven. We can create an SLA-backed policy that restricts failover regions to a whitelist (example: us-east-1, us-west-2). Any emergency cross-region failover outside the whitelist requires a signed emergency authorization and generates an immutable incident record.

Recommended deployment options for Horizon:
- Dedicated (reserved capacity) in US regions with warm-standby workers in EU that do NOT hold PII. This gives predictable throughput and strong isolation.
- Use Customer-Managed Keys (KMS) for at-rest encryption; we support KMS integrations and can work with your key rotation schedule.
- Turn off full-content request logging by default. Enable a separate secure export pipeline if you need forensics copies (exported via secured S3 with access controls).

Attachments: quick one-pager outlining how pinning, warm-standby, and logging configs map to contractual controls (redwood-residency-ops-onepager.pdf).

Next steps I suggest:
- Technical deep-dive with our infra architect to draw a simple network diagram (30–45m).
- Legal/Procurement: Monica to draft SOW addendum language covering residency, logging retention, and emergency failover authorization.

Happy to join a call next week.

Thanks,
Ben Carter
